task_1.title: Differentiate JWT audience mismatch errors
task_1.description: The upgrade makes JWT audience validation errors more specific so callers can distinguish between an invalid audience argument and a token whose audience claim does not satisfy the expected audience.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT audience validation clearly distinguishes a caller-provided invalid audience configuration from the case where a token's audience claim does not match the expected audience.

expectation.grounded: When audience validation runs in PyJWT and the token's `aud` claim does not contain any of the expected audience values, decoding should raise `InvalidAudienceError` with audience-mismatch-specific wording rather than the same generic wording used for invalid audience input by the caller.
expectation.conceptual: Audience validation should report a token audience mismatch as a distinct failure condition, so applications can tell the difference between a bad caller configuration and a token that simply targets a different audience.

constraints.grounded: Keep the failure surfaced as `InvalidAudienceError` for audience validation failures. Only the token-audience mismatch case should become more specific; this change should not alter successful decoding behavior or collapse separate audience-related failure causes back into the same user-visible description.
constraints.conceptual: Do not change which requests succeed or fail. Preserve the existing audience-validation contract while making user-visible error reporting specific enough to distinguish the reason for failure.

behavior: If the expected audience is normalized to one or more values and none of them appears in the token's audience claim, decoding raises `InvalidAudienceError` for an audience mismatch.
The user-visible description for that `InvalidAudienceError` identifies the failure as an audience mismatch instead of using the generic invalid-audience wording.
This makes the token-audience mismatch path observably distinguishable from errors caused by the caller supplying an invalid audience value.
acceptance_criteria: When decoding a token whose `aud` claim does not include the required audience, it should fail with `InvalidAudienceError` and the error text should indicate an audience mismatch.

When an application inspects audience-related decoding failures, it should be able to distinguish a token audience mismatch from a caller-side invalid audience input based on the user-visible error description.
When the token audience matches one of the expected audience values, this change should not introduce any new failure behavior.

task_4.title: Ignore invalid keys when loading JWKS
task_4.description: PyJWT 2.7.0 makes JWKS loading more resilient by ignoring malformed or otherwise unusable keys instead of failing the entire set immediately. Valid keys in a mixed JWKS should remain available, while a JWKS with no usable keys must still fail with a clearer error that can point to missing cryptography support.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that loading a JWKS tolerates invalid or unusable key entries so one bad key does not prevent consumers from using other valid keys in the same set.

expectation.grounded: PyJWKSet construction, including PyJWKSet.from_dict and PyJWKSet.from_json, should ignore individual JWK entries that raise a PyJWTError while being converted into PyJWK objects. The resulting PyJWKSet should retain all usable keys and preserve normal key lookup behavior. If no usable keys remain after filtering, it should raise PyJWKSetError rather than returning an empty usable set, with an error that indicates missing cryptography support may be one cause.
expectation.conceptual: JWKS-loading APIs should accept mixed-quality key sets by skipping entries that cannot be used and continuing with the valid keys that remain. Loading should still fail clearly when the JWKS does not contain any usable keys at all.

constraints.grounded: Do not reject an entire JWKS solely because some entries are malformed, unsupported, or otherwise unusable during PyJWK creation. Continue to raise PyJWKSetError when every entry is unusable or when the set effectively yields zero usable keys, and keep successful key selection behavior unchanged for retained keys.
constraints.conceptual: Partial invalidity in a JWKS must not become a full failure, but a completely unusable JWKS must still surface as an error. Existing successful behavior for valid keys should remain intact.

behavior: When a JWKS contains both valid and invalid key entries, only the valid entries are kept in the loaded key set.
Errors raised while turning an individual JWK into a usable key object are treated as per-entry failures and do not abort loading if other usable keys exist.
If all JWKS entries are unusable, loading fails with PyJWKSetError instead of producing a usable key set.
The failure mode for a fully unusable JWKS is clarified to indicate that missing cryptography support may explain why no keys could be used.
acceptance_criteria: When loading a JWKS that includes at least one usable key and at least one invalid or unsupported key, it should return a PyJWKSet containing the usable key or keys.
When looking up a retained key by key ID after loading a mixed JWKS, it should behave the same as for any other successfully loaded PyJWKSet.
When loading a JWKS in which every key entry is invalid or unusable, it should raise PyJWKSetError.
When a runtime environment lacks support needed to use the provided JWKS keys and no usable keys can be created, the raised PyJWKSetError should make that possible cause clear.

task_2.title: Clarify JWK errors when cryptography is unavailable
task_2.description: The 2.7.0 update makes JWK and JWK set loading failures more actionable when an algorithm depends on the optional cryptography package. Instead of only failing generically, the library now signals that the missing dependency is the likely cause and continues filtering unusable keys in a JWK set before failing only if no usable keys remain.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWK and JWK set loading report actionable failures when a selected algorithm depends on the optional cryptography package, while still preserving usable keys from a set whenever possible.

expectation.grounded: When `PyJWK` resolves an algorithm that belongs to the cryptography-required algorithm set and cryptography support is unavailable, it should raise `PyJWKError` that explicitly points to the missing `cryptography` dependency instead of only surfacing a generic algorithm-resolution failure. When `PyJWKSet` builds from a collection of keys, it should skip keys that fail with `PyJWTError` while continuing to collect usable `PyJWK` entries, and if none remain it should raise `PyJWKSetError` indicating that missing cryptography may be the reason no usable keys were found.
expectation.conceptual: Loading a JWK should clearly tell the caller when the requested key algorithm cannot be used because the optional cryptography package is not installed. Loading a JWK set should tolerate unusable keys, keep any valid keys that can still be used, and only fail with a clear explanation if the entire set is unusable.

constraints.grounded: Do not change successful `PyJWK` or `PyJWKSet` behavior for keys that remain supported in the current environment. Algorithms that do not depend on cryptography must continue to resolve normally, and `PyJWKSet` must only raise a set-level failure after attempting all keys and finding no usable entries.
constraints.conceptual: Existing successful JWK flows should keep working. The change is limited to making dependency-related failures clearer and making JWK set parsing more resilient to unusable keys without hiding a total failure.

behavior: `PyJWK` checks whether the resolved algorithm requires cryptography before constructing the algorithm handler.
If cryptography support is unavailable for a cryptography-backed algorithm, `PyJWK` raises `PyJWKError` that identifies the missing optional dependency as the cause.
`PyJWKSet` ignores keys that fail during JWK conversion with `PyJWTError` instead of aborting immediately on those keys.
If every key in a `PyJWKSet` is unusable after filtering, `PyJWKSet` raises `PyJWKSetError` with guidance that absent cryptography may explain the failure.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller creates a `PyJWK` for a key whose selected algorithm requires cryptography in an environment where cryptography support is unavailable, it should raise `PyJWKError` that clearly indicates the missing dependency.
When a caller creates a `PyJWK` for a key that uses an algorithm supported by the current environment, it should continue to produce a usable JWK object.
When a caller creates a `PyJWKSet` from a mix of usable and unusable keys, it should retain the usable keys rather than failing on the first unusable key covered by `PyJWTError`.
When a caller creates a `PyJWKSet` and none of its keys are usable, it should raise `PyJWKSetError` that explains no usable keys were found and that missing cryptography may be involved.

task_5.title: Advertise Python 3.11 compatibility in package metadata
task_5.description: Version 2.7.0 adds Python 3.11 support metadata so package indexes and compatibility tools can recognize the library as compatible with Python 3.11. This is a packaging and ecosystem visibility update rather than a runtime behavior change.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the library explicitly advertises Python 3.11 compatibility in its published package metadata so ecosystem tools and users can detect support for that Python version.

expectation.grounded: The published distribution metadata should include a Python 3.11 classifier alongside the library's other supported Python version classifiers, allowing package consumers and compatibility services to recognize Python 3.11 support. No public runtime API changes, new error types, or behavioral changes are evidenced by the provided code diff.
expectation.conceptual: The package should clearly signal that it supports Python 3.11 so users and automated tooling can identify the library as compatible with that interpreter version.

constraints.grounded: The update should remain limited to package support metadata for Python 3.11 and should not change existing runtime behavior, public APIs, import paths, return values, warnings, or exception behavior.
constraints.conceptual: This should be a compatibility-advertising update only, without altering how the library behaves for existing users.

behavior: Published package metadata advertises Python 3.11 as a supported interpreter version.
Compatibility-checking tools that rely on package classifiers can identify the library as supporting Python 3.11.
No user-visible runtime behavior changes are introduced by the provided update evidence.
acceptance_criteria: When the library's package metadata is inspected, it should indicate Python 3.11 support among its supported Python versions.
When a compatibility service or packaging client reads the library classifiers, it should recognize the library as compatible with Python 3.11.
When existing runtime library features are used after this update, they should behave the same as before because the change is metadata-only.

task_3.title: Enforce the abstract Algorithm contract
task_3.description: PyJWT 2.7.0 turns Algorithm into an abstract base class and formalizes the required contract for custom JWT algorithms. Code that relied on instantiating the base type or on partially implemented subclasses must now provide a complete concrete algorithm, while the shared base class exposes a hash-digest helper for algorithms that define a hash implementation.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that custom JWT algorithm integrations remain compatible with 2.7.0 by treating Algorithm as an abstract contract rather than an instantiable placeholder, and by providing the full signing, verification, key preparation, and JWK conversion behavior expected by the library.

expectation.grounded: `jwt.algorithms.Algorithm` must behave as an abstract base class. Consumers should only use concrete subclasses that implement `prepare_key`, `sign`, `verify`, `to_jwk`, and `from_jwk`. The base class also exposes `compute_hash_digest(bytes)` for algorithms that define `hash_alg`; calling that helper without a supported hash algorithm should raise `NotImplementedError`.
expectation.conceptual: Custom JWT algorithms should be fully defined concrete components. Applications should no longer rely on creating a generic algorithm object and discovering unsupported operations only when methods are called; incomplete algorithms should be rejected up front, while complete algorithms continue to support signing, verification, key normalization, and JWK import/export.

constraints.grounded: Do not broaden or alter the observable behavior of existing concrete algorithms beyond enforcing the abstract contract. Concrete implementations must continue to expose signature generation as bytes, verification as a boolean result, and JWK conversion through the public `to_jwk` and `from_jwk` methods. Operations that are unsupported for a given algorithm should continue to signal that lack of support through exception behavior when invoked.
constraints.conceptual: Existing working algorithms should keep behaving the same for normal signing, verification, and key conversion flows. The upgrade should tighten the contract for incomplete or placeholder implementations without changing the expected behavior of valid concrete algorithms.

behavior: `Algorithm` can no longer be instantiated directly because it is abstract.
A custom subclass of `Algorithm` must implement key preparation, signing, verification, JWK serialization, and JWK deserialization before it can be used as a concrete algorithm.
`Algorithm.compute_hash_digest(bytes)` provides a shared digest helper for algorithms with a defined `hash_alg`, and it raises `NotImplementedError` when no hash algorithm is available.
Concrete algorithm methods are expected to operate on byte messages and byte signatures, with verification returning a boolean result.
acceptance_criteria: When application code attempts to instantiate `jwt.algorithms.Algorithm` directly, it should fail immediately because the base type is abstract.
When a custom algorithm subclass omits any required abstract member, it should not be usable as a concrete algorithm.
When a concrete custom algorithm implements the full `Algorithm` contract, it should remain usable for key preparation, signing, verification, and JWK conversion.
When `compute_hash_digest` is called on an algorithm that defines a supported `hash_alg`, it should return digest bytes for the supplied input.
When `compute_hash_digest` is called on an algorithm without a hash algorithm, it should raise `NotImplementedError`.

task_6.title: Fix numeric-string iat validation during JWT decode
task_6.description: The 2.7.0 update fixes issued-at claim validation so decode paths treat numeric string `iat` values as valid timestamps instead of failing during comparison. Invalid non-numeric `iat` values and future-issued tokens should continue to raise the appropriate decode-time errors.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT decoding correctly validates the `iat` claim when it is provided as a numeric string, while preserving existing error behavior for malformed or not-yet-valid tokens.

expectation.grounded: `jwt.decode` / `PyJWT.decode` should accept tokens whose `iat` claim can be interpreted as an integer timestamp, including numeric string values, and use that numeric value for issued-at time validation. Decoding should continue to raise `InvalidIssuedAtError` when `iat` is not interpretable as an integer, and should continue to raise `ImmatureSignatureError` when the interpreted `iat` is later than the allowed current time plus leeway.
expectation.conceptual: Token decoding should treat integer-like issued-at values consistently, even when the claim is serialized as text. Users should see successful decoding for valid numeric timestamps, a validation error for malformed issued-at values, and a not-yet-valid error for tokens whose issued-at time is still in the future.

constraints.grounded: This change must remain limited to observable `iat` validation behavior during decode. It must not weaken validation for non-numeric `iat` values, must not suppress future-time checks, and must not require callers to rewrite otherwise valid tokens solely because `iat` is represented as a numeric string.
constraints.conceptual: The update should broaden compatibility for valid issued-at formats without relaxing correctness checks or changing the meaning of future-issued tokens.

behavior: During decode, `iat` values that are integer-like strings are treated as valid issued-at timestamps for comparison against the current time and leeway.
A token with a numeric-string `iat` that is not in the future decodes successfully instead of failing due to type mismatch during validation.
If `iat` cannot be interpreted as an integer, decode raises `InvalidIssuedAtError`.
If the interpreted `iat` is greater than the current time plus leeway, decode raises `ImmatureSignatureError`.
Successful validation of a numeric-string `iat` does not require the decoded payload value itself to be normalized to a different type.
acceptance_criteria: When a token is decoded with an `iat` claim containing digits in string form and that time is not later than the allowed validation window, it should decode successfully.
When a token is decoded with an `iat` claim that is not interpretable as an integer timestamp, it should raise `InvalidIssuedAtError`.
When a token is decoded with an `iat` claim whose interpreted timestamp is in the future beyond leeway, it should raise `ImmatureSignatureError`.
When decoding succeeds for a token with a numeric-string `iat`, the token should not be rejected solely because the claim was encoded as a string.

task_8.title: Clarify jwt.decode verify=False migration guidance
task_8.description: The 2.7.0 update corrects the upgrade guidance for PyJWT's deprecated decode verification flag. It clarifies that migrating old `jwt.decode(..., verify=False)` usage should be described in terms of disabling signature verification through decode options, rather than implying additional expiration-verification configuration changes. No runtime code changes are present in the provided diff.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the upgrade guidance for PyJWT 2.7.0 accurately describes how legacy `jwt.decode(..., verify=False)` usage maps to the 2.x API, so users are not told to change expiration-verification behavior when they only intend to disable signature verification.

expectation.grounded: Documentation and user-facing upgrade guidance must describe the deprecated `jwt.decode(..., verify=False)` pattern as equivalent in PyJWT 2.x to calling `jwt.decode(...)` with `options={"verify_signature": False}`. The guidance should not present `verify_exp` or other validation options as required parts of that migration when describing the old `verify=False` parameter.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to 2.7.0 should be told that the old decode flag for skipping verification maps only to disabling signature verification in the newer options-based API. The upgrade note should not imply that expiration checking behavior also needs to be explicitly changed for that migration.

constraints.grounded: Do not describe any new runtime behavior for `jwt.decode`, because the provided code diff introduces no implementation changes. Keep the requirement limited to correcting the documented mapping of the deprecated `verify` argument to the `options` API.
constraints.conceptual: Treat this upgrade as a clarification of documented behavior, not as a functional change. Existing decode behavior should remain unchanged while the migration guidance becomes accurate and less misleading.

behavior: The provided code diff contains no runtime or API implementation changes between 2.6.0 and 2.7.0.
The release note changes the user-facing interpretation of legacy `jwt.decode(..., verify=False)` migration guidance.

The corrected guidance maps the deprecated `verify=False` usage to disabling signature verification through decode options, without adding expiration-verification configuration as part of that equivalence.
acceptance_criteria: When users read the 2.7.0 upgrade guidance for legacy `jwt.decode(..., verify=False)` usage, it should describe the 2.x equivalent in terms of `options={"verify_signature": False}`.
When users consult the migration note, it should not tell them that they must also configure `verify_exp` in order to match the old `verify=False` behavior.
When comparing 2.6.0 to 2.7.0 using the provided code diff, there should be no expectation of changed production behavior in `jwt.decode`; the update should be understood as documentation-only.

task_7.title: Use sub-second UTC time for JWT time-claim validation
task_7.description: PyJWT 2.7.0 changes JWT time-based claim validation to compare against the current UTC timestamp with fractional-second precision instead of truncating to whole seconds. This makes exp, nbf, and iat checks, including leeway handling, behave accurately near boundary times.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWT decoding validates time-based claims against the actual current UTC time, including fractional seconds, so tokens are not accepted or rejected incorrectly near second boundaries.

expectation.grounded: During jwt.decode and PyJWT.decode claim validation, the current UTC time should be evaluated as a fractional Unix timestamp and used for verify_iat, verify_nbf, and verify_exp comparisons. Leeway, whether passed as a numeric value or timedelta, should be applied against that fractional current time so boundary decisions reflect sub-second elapsed time.
expectation.conceptual: Token validation should honor real wall-clock time rather than rounding down to whole seconds. Around expiration and not-before boundaries, the decode result should change as soon as the actual time crosses the claim threshold after applying any configured leeway.

constraints.grounded: Do not change which claims are validated, when those validations run, or the accepted leeway inputs. Non-time-based claim checks and tokens that are not near time boundaries should continue to behave the same.
constraints.conceptual: Keep the existing validation feature set intact and limit the change to timing precision. The update should only affect borderline cases where sub-second timing matters.

behavior: The current UTC time used during decode-time claim validation includes fractional seconds instead of being truncated to an integer second.
Expiration checks for the exp claim are evaluated against the exact elapsed time, removing up to nearly one second of extra validity caused by rounding.

Issued-at and not-before checks for iat and nbf are evaluated against the same sub-second current time, so future-dated tokens become valid only when the real threshold, adjusted by leeway, has been reached.
Leeway continues to offset time-based validations, but the offset is now applied relative to the precise current timestamp for both numeric and timedelta inputs.
acceptance_criteria: When decoding a token with exp verification enabled and the expiration boundary falls within the current second, it should be accepted or rejected based on the actual UTC timestamp plus any configured leeway, not the start of that second.
When decoding a token with nbf verification enabled, it should remain invalid until the real current UTC time, after applying leeway, reaches the not-before threshold.
When decoding a token with iat verification enabled, a future-issued token should remain invalid until the real current UTC time, after applying leeway, reaches the issued-at threshold.
When leeway is supplied as either a numeric value or a timedelta, the same sub-second-aware comparison behavior should apply to time-based claim validation.
When a token's validation outcome is not near a time boundary, decode behavior and enabled validation options should remain unchanged.

task_10.title: Support custom headers and connection-aware failures in PyJWKClient
task_10.description: The 2.7.0 update expands PyJWKClient so callers can customize outbound JWK set fetch requests with HTTP headers and a request timeout, while network and timeout failures now surface as a connection-specific client error instead of the previous generic fetch error.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that PyJWKClient can be configured for authenticated or customized JWK set fetches by supplying request headers, and that fetch failures caused by connectivity or timeout issues are exposed as a connection-specific error.

expectation.grounded: PyJWKClient should accept optional headers and timeout constructor arguments. When the client fetches the JWK set, it should issue the request using the configured headers and timeout values. If the fetch fails because urllib raises URLError or TimeoutError, the client should raise PyJWKClientConnectionError instead of the previous generic PyJWKClientError used for fetch failures.
expectation.conceptual: Users of PyJWKClient should be able to customize how the library contacts the JWK endpoint, including sending extra HTTP headers and controlling request timeout behavior. When the endpoint cannot be reached or the request times out, the failure should be reported as a dedicated connection-related error rather than a generic client failure.

constraints.grounded: Existing successful JWK set retrieval behavior should remain unchanged aside from using the configured request options. Omitting headers should still allow a normal fetch with no required extra configuration. Only connection-related fetch failures covered by URLError or TimeoutError should be remapped to PyJWKClientConnectionError by this change.
constraints.conceptual: This update should add request customization without changing normal successful JWK retrieval behavior. Default usage should continue to work without extra parameters, and only network-style failures should shift to the more specific error category.

behavior: PyJWKClient exposes a new optional headers argument for outbound JWK set requests.
PyJWKClient exposes a new timeout argument and applies it to JWK set fetches.
JWK set fetches are performed through a request object that includes the configured headers.
Fetch failures caused by URL access errors or request timeouts raise PyJWKClientConnectionError.
Successful fetches still return the parsed JWK set payload for downstream key resolution.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller creates PyJWKClient with custom headers and the client fetches the JWK set, it should send those headers on the outbound HTTP request.
When a caller creates PyJWKClient with a custom timeout, JWK set retrieval should honor that timeout value for the HTTP request.
When JWK set retrieval encounters a URL-related connection failure, the client should raise PyJWKClientConnectionError.
When JWK set retrieval exceeds the configured timeout and a timeout failure occurs, the client should raise PyJWKClientConnectionError.
When JWK set retrieval succeeds, the client should continue to return usable JWK set data without requiring callers to provide headers or timeout values.

task_9.title: Add hash digest support on Algorithm objects
task_9.description: Version 2.7.0 adds a public way to compute the digest associated with a JWT algorithm directly from an Algorithm object. This enables application flows such as token hash validation while defining a clear unsupported case for algorithms that do not have an underlying hash implementation.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications can compute the hash digest associated with a selected JWT Algorithm instance for arbitrary input bytes, and that algorithms without an associated hash algorithm fail in a predictable way instead of exposing undefined behavior.

expectation.grounded: Algorithm instances must provide a public `compute_hash_digest(bytes)` method that returns the raw digest bytes produced by the algorithm's underlying `hash_alg`. The method must work for algorithms whose `hash_alg` is provided either as a `hashlib`-style callable or as a `cryptography.hazmat.primitives.hashes.HashAlgorithm` class. If an Algorithm implementation does not define a usable `hash_alg`, the call must raise `NotImplementedError`.
expectation.conceptual: Callers should be able to ask a JWT algorithm object to hash arbitrary bytes using the same digest family that the algorithm is defined around. If that algorithm does not support hashing, the library should fail explicitly with an unsupported-operation error.

constraints.grounded: This is an additive API and must not alter existing signing, verification, key preparation, or JWK conversion behavior. Digest computation must reflect the algorithm's declared hash implementation and return digest bytes, not an encoded or transformed representation. Unsupported algorithms must raise `NotImplementedError` rather than silently selecting a fallback hash.
constraints.conceptual: The new capability should only add digest access; existing token processing behavior should remain unchanged. Results should be the direct digest output for the requested input, and unsupported algorithms should fail clearly instead of guessing.

behavior: A new public `Algorithm.compute_hash_digest` instance method is available on algorithm objects.
For algorithms with an associated hash implementation, `compute_hash_digest` accepts input bytes and returns the raw digest bytes for that input.
Digest computation supports both standard-library hash constructors and cryptography-backed hash algorithm types.
Algorithms that do not expose an associated hash algorithm raise `NotImplementedError` when `compute_hash_digest` is called.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller invokes `compute_hash_digest` on a JWT Algorithm that has a defined hash algorithm, it should return the raw digest bytes for the supplied byte string.
When the Algorithm's hash support is backed by a cryptography hash algorithm type, the returned digest should match the digest produced by that hash for the same input.
When the Algorithm's hash support is backed by a hashlib-style hash constructor, the returned digest should match that constructor's digest output for the same input.
When `compute_hash_digest` is called on an Algorithm that has no associated hash algorithm, it should raise `NotImplementedError`.

task_11.title: Add overridable JWT payload encode/decode hooks to PyJWT
task_11.description: PyJWT 2.7.0 adds overridable payload serialization and deserialization hooks so custom PyJWT subclasses can support non-default payload formats, while preserving the standard JSON-object behavior and claim validation flow for normal tokens.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `PyJWT` subclasses can customize how JWT payloads are converted to signed bytes and how verified payload bytes are decoded back into application data, so non-standard payload encodings can be supported without breaking the default JWT behavior.

expectation.grounded: `PyJWT.encode()` should obtain the payload bytes through a new overridable `_encode_payload()` hook before signing, and `PyJWT.decode_complete()` should obtain the decoded payload through a new overridable `_decode_payload()` hook after JWS verification and before claim validation. The default hooks must preserve the existing behavior by encoding payloads as compact UTF-8 JSON and decoding payloads as JSON objects, raising `DecodeError` when the payload is invalid JSON or is not a JSON object. Any decoded payload returned from the hook should become the `payload` value in the `decode_complete()` result and the value returned by `decode()`.
expectation.conceptual: Applications that extend `PyJWT` should be able to plug in custom payload formats, such as transformed or compressed payloads, by overriding dedicated payload hooks. Out of the box, standard JWTs should keep working exactly as before: payloads are treated as JSON objects, invalid payload content is rejected with a decode error, and decoded claims remain available through the normal decode APIs.

constraints.grounded: The new hooks must not change the default public behavior for standard JWT payloads. Claim validation must still run on the decoded payload produced by `_decode_payload()`, and successful `decode_complete()` responses must continue to include the decoded payload alongside the verified header and signature data. Custom payload handling must not bypass existing encode options such as header sorting.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade should extend PyJWT rather than redefine it. Existing callers using normal JWT payloads should see no behavioral regression, and custom payload support should fit into the same verification and claim-checking flow that the library already exposes.

behavior: `PyJWT.encode()` now delegates payload byte generation to `_encode_payload()`, allowing subclasses to replace the default payload serialization behavior.
The default `_encode_payload()` implementation serializes the payload as compact JSON encoded to UTF-8 bytes.
`PyJWT.decode_complete()` now delegates payload parsing to `_decode_payload()` after signature verification and before claim validation.
The default `_decode_payload()` implementation parses the verified payload as JSON and raises `DecodeError` if the payload cannot be parsed as JSON or does not decode to a JSON object.
The decoded payload produced by `_decode_payload()` is used for downstream claim validation and is exposed through the normal decode results.
Encoding with custom payload handling still preserves existing encode-time options, including header sorting behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller uses the default `PyJWT` implementation to encode a token, it should continue producing a token from a JSON-object payload without requiring any subclass changes.

When a caller uses the default `PyJWT` implementation to decode a valid standard token, `decode_complete()` should return the decoded payload as a JSON object together with the verified header and signature data.
When the verified payload is invalid JSON under the default decoding behavior, decoding should fail with `DecodeError`.
When the verified payload decodes to a JSON value other than an object under the default decoding behavior, decoding should fail with `DecodeError`.

When a custom `PyJWT` subclass overrides `_encode_payload()` and `_decode_payload()`, the subclass should be able to round-trip tokens using its own payload representation through the standard encode/decode APIs.
When a custom payload decoder is used, claim validation should still run against the decoded payload before the token is returned to the caller.
When `encode()` is called with header sorting options, token generation should still honor that option even if payload encoding is customized.

task_12.title: Expose JWT header ordering control in encode
task_12.description: PyJWT 2.7.0 adds a `sort_headers` option to JWT encoding so callers can preserve header insertion order when needed, while keeping sorted headers as the default. The encode path also now requires payloads to be plain dictionaries and routes payload serialization through an overridable hook.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to PyJWT 2.7.0 lets callers control whether JWT headers are sorted during encoding so existing integrations that depend on header insertion order can opt out of sorting, while preserving the default sorted behavior and enforcing that encoded JWT payloads are JSON-object dictionaries.

expectation.grounded: `api_jwt.encode` / `PyJWT.encode` should accept a `sort_headers` boolean parameter that defaults to `True` and forwards to JWS header serialization. When `sort_headers` is `False`, the encoded JOSE header should retain the caller-provided dictionary order instead of being sorted by key. `encode` should accept only `dict` payloads and raise `TypeError` for non-`dict` mapping-like inputs. Payload serialization should be performed through `_encode_payload`, allowing subclasses to override how payload bytes are produced before signing.
expectation.conceptual: JWT encoding should allow callers to disable automatic header sorting when they need tokens to preserve the order in which header fields were supplied. Existing callers that do not opt out should keep the current sorted-header behavior, and encoding should continue to accept only plain object-style payloads.

constraints.grounded: Omitting `sort_headers` must preserve the existing default of sorted header keys. Disabling header sorting must affect only header key ordering in the encoded token, not payload claim handling or decode behavior. The payload contract remains restricted to `dict` objects representing JSON objects.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must remain backward compatible by default, changing header order only when explicitly requested. It must not broaden payload acceptance beyond normal JSON object dictionaries or change how tokens are interpreted when decoded.

behavior: `PyJWT.encode` exposes a new `sort_headers` option and passes it through to the lower-level JWS encoder.
Header JSON serialization now sorts keys only when `sort_headers` is `True`; when `False`, the emitted JWT header preserves insertion order from the supplied header dictionary.
JWT payload encoding now rejects mapping-like objects that are not actual `dict` instances by raising `TypeError`.
Payload bytes used for signing are produced via `_encode_payload`, creating an overridable extension point for custom payload serialization.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller encodes a token with custom headers and does not provide `sort_headers`, the resulting JWT header segment should remain key-sorted as before.
When a caller encodes a token with `sort_headers=False`, the resulting JWT header segment should preserve the supplied header field order instead of alphabetically sorting it.
When a caller passes a payload container that behaves like a mapping but is not a `dict`, encoding should fail with `TypeError` rather than producing a token.
When a `PyJWT` subclass overrides `_encode_payload`, `encode` should use that customized payload serialization while still honoring the requested header-sorting behavior.

task_13.title: Tighten PyJWT public typing contracts
task_13.description: PyJWT 2.7.0 strengthens the published types for core JWT, JWS, JWK, exception, and utility APIs so strict type checkers can reason about them more accurately while preserving normal library behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to PyJWT 2.7.0 provides stricter and more accurate typing for public APIs and utility helpers without changing expected JWT processing behavior.

expectation.grounded: Public APIs should expose explicit type contracts: `get_default_algorithms()` returns a mapping of algorithm names to `Algorithm` instances; `PyJWT.__init__` accepts an optional options dictionary; `PyJWS.__init__` accepts an optional list of algorithm names and an optional options dictionary; `PyJWTSetWithTimestamp.get_jwk_set()` returns `PyJWKSet`; `PyJWTSetWithTimestamp.get_timestamp()` returns `float`; `JWKSetCache` construction and `put()` return no value; `MissingRequiredClaimError` is initialized with a claim name string and remains string-convertible. Utility helpers `force_bytes`, `base64url_decode`, and `from_base64url_uint` should continue accepting `str` and `bytes` inputs and returning decoded `bytes` or `int` values. `jwt.help.info()` should continue reporting the installed `cryptography` version when available and an empty version string when it is not installed.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should make the library safer to use in strictly typed Python projects by publishing clearer input and output types for its public APIs, while keeping the same observable JWT, JWK, and helper behavior for existing callers.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the existing constructor shapes or helper return categories for `PyJWT`, `PyJWS`, algorithm lookup, JWK cache accessors, or claim-related exceptions. `base64url_decode()` and `from_base64url_uint()` must keep accepting both text and byte inputs. `jwt.help.info()` must not fail when `cryptography` is absent and must still return the same metadata structure.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must remain backward compatible for normal callers: JWT workflows should keep working, helper functions should remain usable with text or byte inputs, and environment introspection should still succeed whether optional crypto support is installed or not.

behavior: `get_default_algorithms()` now has an explicit typed contract for a dictionary of algorithm implementations.
`PyJWT` and `PyJWS` constructors now publish typed optional configuration inputs, including a list of algorithm names for `PyJWS`.
JWK set timestamp wrapper accessors now expose concrete return types for the cached `PyJWKSet` and its timestamp.
`force_bytes()`, `base64url_decode()`, and `from_base64url_uint()` normalize `str` and `bytes` inputs through a shared byte-conversion path while continuing to return decoded bytes or integers.
`raw_to_der_signature()` guarantees a concrete `bytes` return value.
`jwt.help.info()` continues to report a `cryptography` version string when the dependency is present and an empty version string when it is not.
`MissingRequiredClaimError` now publishes explicit types for its claim argument and string conversion.
acceptance_criteria: When a typed application calls `get_default_algorithms()`, it should be able to treat the result as a mapping of algorithm names to algorithm objects.
When a caller instantiates `PyJWT` with no options or with an options dictionary, it should behave the same as before while exposing a typed options mapping.
When a caller instantiates `PyJWS` with no algorithms, with a list of algorithm names, and optionally with options, it should continue to initialize successfully with those inputs.
When code reads a cached JWK set wrapper, `get_jwk_set()` should return the wrapped JWK set object and `get_timestamp()` should return the recorded timestamp value.
When `base64url_decode()` or `from_base64url_uint()` receives either `str` or `bytes`, it should continue decoding valid values and return `bytes` or `int` respectively.
When DER signatures are produced from raw signatures, the returned value should be a `bytes` object.

When `jwt.help.info()` runs in environments with or without `cryptography` installed, it should return the usual metadata dictionary and report either the installed version or an empty version string.
When `MissingRequiredClaimError` is created with a claim name, converting the exception to text should still describe the missing claim.

task_15.title: Add configurable timeout and headers to PyJWKClient JWKS fetches
task_15.description: The PyJWT 2.7.0 upgrade changes PyJWKClient network fetching so JWKS downloads no longer wait indefinitely by default. PyJWKClient now applies a default timeout, lets callers override that timeout and attach request headers, and treats URL and timeout failures as connection-related fetch errors.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that PyJWKClient JWKS retrieval uses a finite default network timeout, allows callers to provide custom HTTP headers and a custom timeout for JWKS requests, and reports network or timeout failures as connection-related fetch errors instead of hanging indefinitely.

expectation.grounded: PyJWKClient should accept optional `headers` and `timeout` constructor arguments. When fetching JWKS data, it should issue the request with the configured headers and timeout, default the timeout to 30 seconds when none is provided, return the decoded JWKS payload on success, and raise `PyJWKClientConnectionError` when the fetch fails due to URL access or timeout errors.
expectation.conceptual: Applications using PyJWKClient should be able to control request metadata and how long JWKS retrieval waits before failing. If the JWKS endpoint is unreachable or takes too long, the client should fail with a connection-style error rather than block without a timeout.

constraints.grounded: The change must preserve successful JWKS retrieval behavior apart from adding request headers and timeout handling. Default usage of PyJWKClient without explicit headers or timeout should continue to work, but with a finite timeout. Failures caused by URL access errors or request timeouts must be surfaced through the JWKS client error path.
constraints.conceptual: Existing successful JWKS lookups should keep working, while the upgrade adds safer network behavior and configurable request options. The new behavior should only affect request configuration and failure handling for remote JWKS fetches.

behavior: PyJWKClient uses a 30-second default timeout for JWKS HTTP requests when no timeout is supplied.
PyJWKClient accepts caller-provided HTTP headers and includes them in outbound JWKS fetch requests.
PyJWKClient accepts a caller-provided timeout value and applies it to the JWKS fetch request.
Successful JWKS fetches still return the parsed JWKS document.
JWKS fetch failures caused by URL errors or request timeouts raise `PyJWKClientConnectionError`.
acceptance_criteria: When an application constructs PyJWKClient without specifying a timeout and fetches JWKS data, the request should use a finite default timeout instead of waiting indefinitely.
When an application constructs PyJWKClient with custom headers and fetches JWKS data, the outbound JWKS request should include those headers.
When an application constructs PyJWKClient with a custom timeout and fetches JWKS data, the outbound JWKS request should use that timeout value.
When the JWKS endpoint responds successfully, PyJWKClient should return the JWKS payload as usual.
When the JWKS fetch encounters a URL access failure or exceeds the timeout, PyJWKClient should raise `PyJWKClientConnectionError`.

task_16.title: Differentiate JWKS connection failures in PyJWKClient
task_16.description: PyJWT 2.7.0 adds a dedicated PyJWKClientConnectionError so JWKS fetch failures caused by connectivity problems can be distinguished from other JWK client errors. The JWKS request path also uses the client's configured headers and timeout when opening the remote endpoint.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that JWKS retrieval through PyJWKClient clearly distinguishes connection-related failures from other JWK client failures so applications can detect transient network issues, handle them separately, and safely retry when appropriate.

expectation.grounded: PyJWKClient should raise PyJWKClientConnectionError when JWKS retrieval encounters URLError or TimeoutError during fetch operations, including flows reached through methods such as get_signing_key_from_jwt(). PyJWKClientConnectionError should remain a subtype of PyJWKClientError so existing broad error handling continues to work. JWKS HTTP fetches should be issued using the client's configured headers and timeout settings.
expectation.conceptual: When PyJWKClient cannot reach the JWKS endpoint because of a network or timeout problem, callers should receive a dedicated connection-oriented exception instead of a generic client failure. Existing code that already handles the broader JWK client error family should remain compatible, and outbound JWKS requests should honor the client's configured request settings.

constraints.grounded: Only connection-oriented JWKS fetch failures should be reclassified as PyJWKClientConnectionError; other PyJWKClient failure modes should continue to surface through their existing error behavior. Successful JWKS fetches should continue to return parsed key set data, and PyJWKClientConnectionError must be catchable via PyJWKClientError.
constraints.conceptual: The change should narrow error reporting for transport failures without changing unrelated failure semantics or breaking existing consumers that catch the broader client exception type.

behavior: PyJWKClient introduces a new public exception type, PyJWKClientConnectionError, for JWKS endpoint connectivity failures.
When JWKS retrieval raises URLError or TimeoutError, PyJWKClient should surface PyJWKClientConnectionError instead of the generic PyJWKClientError.
Higher-level signing-key lookup flows that trigger a JWKS download, including get_signing_key_from_jwt(), should expose connection failures as PyJWKClientConnectionError.
JWKS fetches should open the remote request using the PyJWKClient instance's configured headers and timeout values.
PyJWKClientConnectionError remains within the existing PyJWKClientError hierarchy for backward-compatible broad exception handling.
acceptance_criteria: When application code calls a PyJWKClient method that needs to download JWKS data and the remote endpoint is unreachable, it should raise PyJWKClientConnectionError.
When a JWKS download attempt times out, the caller should receive PyJWKClientConnectionError rather than a generic PyJWKClientError.
When existing application code catches PyJWKClientError, connection-related JWKS failures should still be caught through that base class.
Given a PyJWKClient configured with custom headers or a timeout, when it performs a JWKS HTTP fetch, the request should use those configured values.
When JWKS retrieval succeeds, PyJWKClient should continue returning the parsed key set data instead of changing successful behavior.

task_18.title: Add dictionary output option to JWK serialization
task_18.description: Version 2.7.0 extends JWK serialization so callers can request a native dictionary from `Algorithm.to_jwk()` instead of always receiving JSON text. The existing string return behavior remains the default for backward compatibility.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading to 2.7.0 can obtain JWK data directly as a native mapping from `Algorithm.to_jwk()` without breaking existing code that expects the legacy JSON string output.

expectation.grounded: Expose an optional `as_dict` keyword argument on `Algorithm.to_jwk()` and the concrete `HMACAlgorithm`, `RSAAlgorithm`, `ECAlgorithm`, and `OKPAlgorithm` implementations. When `as_dict=True`, `to_jwk` should return a JWK dictionary; when omitted or `False`, it should continue returning the serialized JWK as `str`. The dictionary form should contain the same JWK members that the string form would encode for the same key material.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to choose whether JWK export returns JSON text or an already-parsed mapping, while preserving the same key information and keeping existing code paths unchanged by default.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the default return type of existing `to_jwk()` calls. Do not alter the JWK fields produced for HMAC, RSA, EC, or OKP keys beyond the container type. Existing key validation and failure behavior for unsupported or invalid key objects should remain intact, including raising `InvalidKeyError` where that was already the observable outcome.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade must add an opt-in output format, not a new serialization format or a breaking API change. Apart from returning a mapping when requested, JWK export should behave the same as before.

behavior: `Algorithm.to_jwk()` accepts an optional `as_dict` flag in 2.7.0.
Calling `to_jwk(..., as_dict=True)` returns a native JWK dictionary instead of JSON text.
Calling `to_jwk(...)` without `as_dict`, or with `as_dict=False`, still returns the JSON string form for backward compatibility.
The new `as_dict` behavior applies across HMAC, RSA, EC, and OKP algorithm implementations.
The returned dictionary contains the same JWK content that would otherwise be emitted in the JSON string for the same key.
Invalid or unsupported asymmetric key objects continue to fail with the existing observable validation behavior rather than silently producing JWK output.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller invokes `to_jwk()` on an algorithm instance without `as_dict`, it should return a string containing the JWK JSON representation, as in prior versions.
When a caller invokes `to_jwk(..., as_dict=True)` on an HMAC algorithm, it should return a dictionary representing the same octet JWK that the string form would contain.

When a caller invokes `to_jwk(..., as_dict=True)` on RSA, EC, or OKP public or private key objects, it should return a dictionary with the same public and private JWK members that are present in the legacy string output for that key.
When the same key is serialized with and without `as_dict=True`, the only externally visible difference should be whether the result is a mapping or JSON text.
When `to_jwk` is given an invalid RSA, EC, or OKP key object, it should preserve the prior failure behavior instead of returning a dictionary or changing the validation contract.

task_14.title: Expand typed key and JWK support across PyJWT APIs
task_14.description: PyJWT 2.7.0 broadens typed support across its decoding and algorithm APIs so static type checkers better reflect the key objects, byte inputs, and helper return shapes the library supports. The update also adds structured JWK export for HMAC secrets while preserving existing validation and error behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to PyJWT 2.7.0 provides more accurate support for supported key objects, byte-based JWT inputs, and JWK helper usage so typed applications can use the library without false type conflicts. Ensure that existing token verification, claim validation, and invalid-key handling semantics remain unchanged.

expectation.grounded: Public decoding entry points `PyJWS.decode()` and `PyJWS.decode_complete()` should accept JWT values as `str` or `bytes` and verification keys as serialized key material or supported cryptography public key objects. Algorithm implementations should expose precise `prepare_key()`, `sign()`, and `verify()` contracts for HMAC, RSA, EC, and OKP/EdDSA key material. `HMACAlgorithm.to_jwk()` should support returning either a JSON string or a JWK mapping via `as_dict`, and `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk()` should accept either representation. Header retrieval through `PyJWS.get_unverified_header()` should remain a mapping result, and existing exception types such as `InvalidKeyError`, `InvalidSignatureError`, `InvalidTokenError`, `ExpiredSignatureError`, `ImmatureSignatureError`, and `MissingRequiredClaimError` should continue to signal the same validation failures.
expectation.conceptual: The library should accurately advertise the token, key, and helper input forms it supports so typed Python applications can decode and verify JWTs without unnecessary casting or wrapper code. JWK helper APIs should support both serialized and structured forms where applicable, while all existing validation outcomes stay consistent.

constraints.grounded: Do not narrow accepted key material for HMAC, RSA, EC, or OKP algorithms. Serialized PEM or SSH inputs and supported cryptography key objects must continue to flow through the same key preparation and verification logic. Asymmetric keys used with HMAC must still be rejected with `InvalidKeyError`; invalid signatures must still raise `InvalidSignatureError`; non-string `kid` values must still raise `InvalidTokenError`; and expiration, not-before, audience, issued-at, and required-claim validation must preserve their existing failure behavior.
constraints.conceptual: This upgrade should improve typing precision and helper ergonomics without changing how valid tokens succeed or how invalid tokens, headers, claims, and keys are rejected.

behavior: `PyJWS.decode()` and `PyJWS.decode_complete()` formally support JWT input supplied as either text or bytes and verification keys supplied as either serialized key material or supported public key objects.
Algorithm classes now align their callable contracts with the concrete key types they already handle for HMAC, RSA, EC, and EdDSA operations.
`HMACAlgorithm.to_jwk()` can return a structured JWK mapping when `as_dict=True`; without that option it continues to return a JSON-serialized JWK string.
`HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk()` accepts either a serialized JWK string or an equivalent mapping object and returns the decoded secret bytes.
Header access through `PyJWS.get_unverified_header()` remains a dictionary-like result with string keys, and the decode path continues to use prepared keys for signature verification.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller exports an HMAC secret with `HMACAlgorithm.to_jwk(..., as_dict=True)`, it should receive a JWK mapping instead of a serialized JSON string.
When a caller exports an HMAC secret with `HMACAlgorithm.to_jwk()` without requesting a mapping result, it should continue to receive a JSON-serialized JWK string.
When a caller passes a serialized HMAC JWK string or an equivalent mapping object to `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk()`, both forms should be accepted and should produce the same secret bytes.

When `PyJWS.decode()` or `PyJWS.decode_complete()` is called with a JWT provided as bytes and a supported asymmetric public key object, the token should proceed through the normal verification path without requiring manual conversion to string key material.

When token headers, claims, signatures, or keys are invalid, the library should continue to raise the same validation exception families instead of silently accepting the input or changing failure semantics.

task_17.title: Expand key typing and JWK interoperability in PyJWT 2.7.0
task_17.description: PyJWT 2.7.0 broadens the public JWT/JWS/JWK API surface to recognize the full set of supported key forms, adds structured JWK serialization and deserialization options, tightens payload shape validation during JWT encoding and decoding, and reports clearer failures when cryptography-backed JWK algorithms cannot be used.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to PyJWT 2.7.0 supports all allowed signing and verification key forms across JWT and JWS APIs, allows supported keys to round-trip through JWK APIs as either JSON text or dictionary data, and surfaces clear failures for unsupported payload shapes or unusable JWK inputs.

expectation.grounded: `jwt.encode`, `jwt.decode`, `PyJWT.encode`, `PyJWT.decode`, `PyJWS.encode`, and `PyJWS.decode` should accept supported key objects in addition to string and bytes keys, including RSA, elliptic-curve, Ed25519, and Ed448 keys where applicable. `Algorithm.to_jwk` and concrete algorithm implementations should support returning either a JWK JSON string or a JWK dictionary via `as_dict`, and `from_jwk` should accept either representation. `PyJWK` should raise `PyJWKError` when the selected JWK algorithm requires `cryptography` but that dependency is unavailable, and `PyJWKSet` should raise `PyJWKSetError` when no usable keys remain. `PyJWT.encode` should require a `dict` payload, and payload decoding should raise `DecodeError` for invalid JSON payload text or JSON values that are not objects.
expectation.conceptual: The upgraded library should let callers use any supported key object or encoded key material directly with the public JWT/JWS APIs, should interoperate cleanly with JWK data in either serialized or already-parsed form, and should fail early with explicit JWT/JWK errors when payload content or key material is not usable.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress existing signing, verification, or JWK round-trip behavior for valid string or bytes keys. HMAC secret handling must continue rejecting asymmetric PEM or SSH material with `InvalidKeyError`. RSA, EC, and OKP verification should preserve the existing boolean success/failure contract for invalid signatures. `NoneAlgorithm.to_jwk` and `NoneAlgorithm.from_jwk` remain unsupported.
constraints.conceptual: Existing valid token workflows must continue to work, invalid signatures must still be treated as verification failures rather than successful decodes, and unsafe or unsupported key types must continue to be rejected instead of being coerced silently.

behavior: JWT and JWS encode/decode entry points accept the full set of supported key inputs for each algorithm, including `cryptography` private and public key objects alongside string and bytes key material.
Supported algorithm `to_jwk` methods can return either serialized JWK JSON or an in-memory JWK dictionary, and supported `from_jwk` paths accept either input form.
`PyJWT.encode` rejects payload values that are not real JSON-object dictionaries.
JWT payload decoding raises `DecodeError` when the payload text is not valid JSON or when the decoded JSON value is not an object.
`PyJWK` reports a `PyJWKError` when a JWK selects an algorithm that depends on `cryptography` and the dependency is not installed.
`PyJWKSet` skips unusable keys and raises `PyJWKSetError` if the set contains no usable keys after filtering.
Algorithms that define a hash backend expose `compute_hash_digest(bytes)` to return the raw digest bytes for the configured hash algorithm.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller signs with a supported RSA, EC, Ed25519, or Ed448 private key object, the public encode API should accept that object directly without requiring PEM conversion first.
When a caller verifies with the corresponding supported public key object, the public decode API should accept that object directly and preserve normal verification success or failure behavior.
When `to_jwk(..., as_dict=True)` is called for a supported key or secret, it should return a JWK dictionary; when `as_dict` is omitted or false, it should return JSON text for the same JWK data.
When `from_jwk` receives either JWK JSON text or an equivalent parsed JWK dictionary, it should reconstruct usable key material for the selected algorithm.
When `jwt.encode` receives a payload that is mapping-like but not a `dict`, it should raise `TypeError` instead of encoding it.
When decoded payload content is not a valid JSON object, decode should raise `DecodeError`.
When a JWK references an algorithm that requires `cryptography` and that dependency is unavailable, constructing `PyJWK` should raise `PyJWKError`.
When all keys in a JWK set are unusable, constructing `PyJWKSet` should raise `PyJWKSetError`.
